lead.t: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) correlate with CIN 2 or 3, which are less likely to regress and are therefore resected.

snip.t: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) correlate with CIN 2 or 3, which are less likely to regress and are therefore resected.
The cytopathology report indicates the presence of severely dysplastic cells (high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, or HSIL).
Progression through a spectrum of pre-invasive lesions: Low-grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (LSIL) → High-grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (HSIL).

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: HSIL is a pre‑cancerous change of the cervical epithelium with severe dysplasia. It is identified on cytology or histology and requires prompt evaluation to prevent invasive cancer.

sections.p: HSIL denotes severe dysplasia or carcinoma in situ of the squamous epithelium, most often of the cervix. Diagnosis is made by Pap smear showing atypical cells with a high nuclear‑to‑cytoplasmic ratio, or by colposcopic biopsy confirming full‑thickness atypia.
b: Cytology: HSIL on Pap smear (ASC‑H, HSIL)
Histology: full‑thickness dysplasia, no stromal invasion

t.b: Does the sample show HSIL? Positive indicates severe dysplasia; negative does not rule out lesion if sampling was poor.
Confirms HSIL and excludes invasive cancer; if unavailable, refer for excisional procedure.

sections.p: HSIL is a grade 2–3 lesion in the Bethesda system and corresponds to CIN 2–3 in the WHO classification. It is pre‑invasive; staging applies only if invasion is found (FIGO stage 0).
b: CIN 2 = moderate dysplasia, CIN 3 = severe dysplasia/carcinoma in situ
FIGO stage 0 = HSIL without invasion

sections.p: Persistent infection with high‑risk human papillomavirus (HPV) types 16, 18, 31, 33 is the primary cause. Co‑factors that impair immunity increase risk, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: HPV 16/18 infection (most common)
Immunosuppression (HIV, transplant, malnutrition)
Smoking
Long‑term oral contraceptives

sections.p: HSIL is usually asymptomatic and discovered on routine screening. When symptoms occur, they may include post‑coital bleeding or a visible cervical lesion on speculum exam.
b: Often no symptoms; detected by Pap smear
Possible intermenstrual or post‑coital bleeding

sections.p: After a cytology report of HSIL, colposcopy with directed biopsy is the next step. Endocervical sampling and HPV genotyping help risk stratify.
b: Colposcopy to visualise lesion and obtain tissue
HPV genotyping for high‑risk types

t.b: Is a high‑risk HPV type present? Positive supports HSIL etiology; negative suggests alternative cause or sampling error.
Is disease extending into the endocervical canal? Positive indicates need for more extensive excision.

sections.p: If invasive cancer develops, patients may present with a larger exophytic mass, persistent bleeding, or pelvic pain. Untreated HSIL can progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma within 5–10 years.
b: Rapidly enlarging cervical mass
Uncontrolled vaginal bleeding
Pelvic pain or urinary obstruction

sections.p: Treat the lesion by excisional or ablative methods, then monitor for recurrence. Choice depends on lesion size, patient age, desire for fertility, and resource availability.
b: Loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) – removes full thickness of transformation zone; preferred for most HSIL.
Cold‑knife conization – surgical excision; used when LEEP unavailable or margins needed.
Ablative therapy (cryotherapy, laser) – for small lesions where histology not required.

sections.p: After treatment, repeat cytology and HPV testing at 6 months, then annually for at least 3 years. Primary prevention is HPV vaccination; secondary prevention is regular screening.
b: Pap smear at 6 months post‑procedure
HPV testing at 12 months if initial test was positive
Vaccinate girls (and boys) before sexual debut

sections.p: Conditions that can mimic HSIL on cytology or colposcopy.
b: Low‑grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) – milder dysplasia, lower cancer risk.
Atypical glandular cells – arise from endocervical columnar epithelium, not squamous.
Inflammatory/reactive changes – may cause atypia but lack true dysplasia.

sections.p: Certain factors may give false‑negative or false‑positive findings.
b: Sampling error – inadequate cells can miss HSIL.
HPV test negative in HSIL caused by non‑high‑risk types (rare).
Inflammation can obscure colposcopic view, leading to under‑diagnosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in lesion size or new pelvic pain
Fever with foul‑smelling discharge (suggests infection after procedure)

faq.a: Spontaneous regression occurs in a minority, especially in younger women, but the risk of progression to cancer remains high, so treatment is recommended.

faq.q: Is HPV vaccination useful after HSIL is diagnosed?
faq.a: Vaccination does not treat existing infection but protects against other high‑risk types and reduces future lesions.
Excisional procedures can increase the risk of cervical insufficiency; counseling and obstetric follow‑up are advised for women desiring pregnancy.

exam: Describe the cytologic criteria that define HSIL on a Pap smear.
Explain why high‑risk HPV infection is the primary cause of HSIL and list two co‑factors that increase risk.
Outline the management algorithm for a patient with HSIL diagnosed on cytology.
